title: Boats and Demons Carved in Rock
place: Lake Onega, Pudozhsky District, Republic of Karelia, Russia
text: Between about 4500 and 3500 BCE, Neolithic hunter-fisher-gatherers in Karelia carved more than 4,500 petroglyphs into rocks at Lake Onega and by the White Sea, 300 km apart. The Onega carvings show birds, forest animals, figures interpreted as demons, and sun and moon signs, while the White Sea panels depict boats, hunting scenes and animal and human footprints.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Petroglyphs of Lake Onega and the White Sea

title: Granite Cairns Above the Sea
text: On a rocky ridge near the Gulf of Bothnia, Bronze Age people piled granite boulders into 33 burial cairns, with no earth fill, between about 1500 and 500 BCE. One rare square cairn is nicknamed the 'Church Floor'. The cairns are linked to sun worship spreading from Scandinavia and may have marked a kin group's land, a custom thought to have come with farming.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Bronze Age Burial Site of Sammallahdenmäki

title: Greek Traders on the Boh Estuary
place: Olbia, near Parutyne, Mykolaiv Oblast, Ukraine
text: Greek settlers from Miletus and other Ionian cities founded Olbia on the Boh River estuary in the early 6th century BC. They traded wine, olive oil, fine dishes, cloth and glassware with Scythians and other steppe peoples in exchange for grain, cattle, wool, fish and slaves. To help trade, the city minted its own bronze, silver and occasionally gold coins.

source.name: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Olbia

title: Vineyards of a Crimean Greek City
text: Dorian Greeks founded Tauric Chersonese in south-west Crimea in the 5th century BCE and laid out its streets on a grid. Its farmland was divided into some 400 equal plots, many planted with vineyards whose wine the city exported. By the 3rd century AD it was known as the most productive wine centre of the Black Sea, trading with Greeks, Romans, Byzantines and peoples to the north.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Ancient City of Tauric Chersonese and its Chora

title: A Trading Town on the Don
place: Tanais, near Rostov-on-Don, Rostov Oblast, Russia
text: At the beginning of the 3rd century BC, Greeks of the Bosporan Kingdom founded Tanais near the mouth of the river of the same name, today's Don. It became a trade centre between steppe nomads and Greeks, home to a mixed population of Greeks, Sarmatians and Maeotians. Goths destroyed it in the mid-3rd century AD, and digging at the site began in 1853.

source.name: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Tanais

title: Amber Gatherers Puzzled by Rome
place: Eastern Baltic shore (Sambia coast), Kaliningrad Oblast, Russia
text: In his Germania, written in 98, the Roman historian Tacitus described the Aestii on the eastern shore of the 'Suevic sea'. He called them the only people who gathered amber, which they named 'glesum', in the shallows and on the shore. Useless to them, it was brought to Rome in shapeless lumps, and the Aestii marvelled at the price they received.

source.name: Perseus Digital Library (Tufts University): Tacitus, Germania, chapter 45 (trans. Church and Brodribb)

title: A Gothic King Facing the Huns
place: Between the Don and Dniester rivers, Ukraine
text: Ermanaric, king of the Ostrogoths, ruled a vast empire in Ukraine that apparently stretched between the Don and Dniester rivers, feared by neighbouring peoples. When the Huns invaded in the 370s, he despaired of resisting them and took his own life. His kingdom was destroyed, and his people were subject to the Huns for about 75 years. Legends about him spread into English and Norse literature.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ermanaric

title: Ladoga, Gateway of the North
text: Tree-ring dating shows the first wooden houses at Ladoga, on the Volkhov River near Lake Ladoga, were built no later than 753 CE. Throughout the Viking Age, Scandinavian traders, craftsmen and farmers reached it by sea through the Gulf of Finland and the Neva River. In the early eleventh century, Yaroslav the Wise gave the area to his wife, Ingegerd Olofsdotter, as a semi-autonomous earldom.

source.name: Cambridge University Press (The Global North, ed. Carol Symes): N. V. Grigorjeva, Archaeological Evidence for Staraya Ladoga as an Early Scandinavian Emporium

title: White Stone Cathedral of Vladimir
text: Built in 1158 inside Vladimir's kremlin, the Cathedral of the Assumption was meant to be the religious centre of all Russia. Its facade is divided into five sections by columns and covered in carved reliefs. Mongols destroyed most of its 12th-century frescoes in 1238, but in 1408 the painters Andrei Rublev and Daniil Chernii added new murals, including a famous Last Judgment.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: White Monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal

title: A Princess-Nun's Jewelled Cross
text: Princess Predslava of Polotsk took monastic vows as Euphrosynia and later led a nunnery. Around 1161 she ordered master Lazar Bogsha to make a cross holding relics of saints and particles of the Holy Sepulchre, covered with gold plates, precious stones and pearls, with his autograph inscribed at the bottom. Moved to the Mogilev Museum in 1928, it later disappeared without a trace.

source.name: Saint Petersburg State University, Medieval Russian Princesses project: Predslava of Polotsk

title: Lithuania's First and Only King
text: Mindaugas, seen as the founder of the Lithuanian state, imposed himself over rival nobles, including his own brother and nephews. He accepted baptism from the Livonian Knights in 1250 or 1251, easing pressure from the west, and in 1253 received a royal crown from Pope Innocent IV. He later returned to paganism and was murdered by Samogitian rivals in 1263.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Mindaugas

title: An ABC Book for Finnish Readers
text: Mikael Agricola, who had studied under Luther at Wittenberg, published his first book, the reading primer Abckiria, probably in 1543. Only pieces of two pages of that first edition survive, but in 1966 eight missing pages turned up in a library in Västerås, Sweden, completing the text. Later Bishop of Turku, Agricola is called the father of written Finnish.

source.name: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland: Mikael Agricola's anniversary

title: The Radziwills' Castle at Nesvizh
text: From 1583 until 1939 the powerful Radziwill family built and kept a castle complex at Nesvizh in central Belarus. Its ten connected buildings, including a palace, family archive and arsenal, ring a six-sided courtyard inside a moat, with a dam leading to the domed Corpus Christi church. Artists from Belarus, Poland, Italy and Germany working there formed a new architectural school.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Architectural, Residential and Cultural Complex of the Radziwill Family at Nesvizh

title: A Cossack Hetman Sparks a Revolution
text: At the end of December 1647 Bohdan Khmelnytsky left for the Zaporizhia with just 300 to 500 men and was elected hetman there, starting a Cossack uprising that quickly became a national revolution. By 1648 Polish officials warned that the Cossacks wanted to rule in Ukraine. After his victories, people in Kyiv hailed him as a Moses and liberator of the Rus' people.

source.name: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Khmelnytsky, Bohdan

title: Twenty-Two Wooden Domes
place: Kizhi Island, Lake Onega, Republic of Karelia, Russia
text: After lightning burned the old churches on Kizhi Island in 1693, new ones rose on the very same spot. Tree-ring dating places the Church of the Transfiguration after 1713-14. Rising 37 m and crowned with 22 bulb-shaped domes, it was used only in summer. Local legend says Master Nestor built it without nails, using nothing but an axe.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Kizhi Pogost

title: Measuring the Earth From Tartu
text: The Tartu Observatory, then known as Dorpat, was the starting point of a huge chain of survey triangles observed between 1816 and 1855 under astronomer F. G. W. Struve. Running 2,820 km from near Norway's North Cape to the Black Sea, it was designed to pin down the size and shape of the Earth. Today 34 of its 265 main stations are World Heritage.

source.name: International Federation of Surveyors (FIG): First for Surveyors and a first for World Heritage

title: A Country Doctor Builds an Epic
text: While working as district medical officer in Kajaani, Elias Lönnrot made trips to hear folk singers, among them Arhippa Perttunen of Archangel Karelia in 1834. He combined different versions of poems on the same subject into one story. The first Kalevala, its preface signed on February 28, 1835, had 32 poems and 12,078 lines, and only 500 copies were printed.

source.name: Kalevala Society: Elias Lönnrot's Kalevala process

title: A Steppe Saved Forever
text: In 1898 Friedrich Falz-Fein ordered that a large plot of feather-grass steppe at Askania-Nova be conserved forever. His zoo there let animals such as zebras, ostriches and saiga antelope roam partly free, and he helped capture rare Przewalski's horses in Mongolia for a herd. It became Ukraine's oldest nature preserve, though Russian forces took control of it in March 2023.

source.name: Askania-Nova Biosphere Reserve (official site)

source2.name: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Askaniia-Nova Biosphere Reserve

title: Finnish Women Win the Ballot
text: After the General Strike of 1905, Finland confirmed a one-chamber parliament in 1906 and gave women the right both to vote and to stand for election, the first European country to do so. Married women were freed from having their husbands act as their guardians. In the first parliamentary elections, in 1907, nineteen women became Members of Parliament.

source.name: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland: Finland - unquestionably a pioneer of democracy

title: A Symphony for a Starving City
text: Dmitri Shostakovich began his Seventh Symphony in besieged Leningrad and finished it in February 1942. The score was flown into the city over German lines, and conductor Karl Eliasberg pushed a starving orchestra through rehearsals; musicians fainted from hunger or cold, and three died. On August 9 the haggard players performed it in the city Hitler had claimed would fall that month.

source.name: NPR (via Texas Public Radio): Amid Hunger And Cold, An Unforgettable Symphony Premiere

title: Scythian Gold Under a Burial Mound
place: Tovsta Mohyla, near Pokrov, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Ukraine
text: In 1971 archaeologist Borys Mozolevsky excavated Tovsta Mohyla, a Scythian burial mound of the 4th century BC. Its untouched side vault held a noblewoman and a child, and the mound gave up more than 600 gold objects. The star was a gold pectoral made by Greek masters around 370-360 BCE, showing griffins attacking horses and a boy milking a sheep.

source.name: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Tovsta Mohyla

source2.name: National Museum of the History of Ukraine (Google Arts & Culture): The Pectoral from Tovsta Mohyla

title: Holding Hands Across Three Countries
text: On August 23, 1989, people in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania formed a human chain 600 km long. The date marked 50 years since the 1939 German-Soviet non-aggression pact and its secret protocol. UNESCO calls it a unique and peaceful demonstration that united the three countries in their drive for freedom, and its documents joined the Memory of the World register in 2009.

source.name: UNESCO Memory of the World: The Baltic Way - Human Chain Linking Three States in Their Drive for Freedom
